title: Different languages, similar encoding efficiency: Comparable information rates across the human communicative niche
authors: Christophe Coupé, Yoon Mi Oh, Dan Dediu, François Pellegrino
key_findings: Science Advances. 17 languages incl. Thai; 170 native speakers (10 per language) read 15 short daily-life texts aloud.
Speech rate = canonical syllables / speech duration excluding pauses >150 ms; overall mean 6.63 syllables/s (SD 1.15); individual speakers ~4.3-9.1 syll/s.
Faster languages carry less information per syllable; information rate converges near 39 bits/s.
Information density 4.8 (Basque) to 8.0 (Vietnamese) bits/syllable; secondary sources place Thai among the slower-rate languages.
practical_applications: Upper-bound sanity check for read speech; Thai-specific value is in the supplement (not read) - calibrate from our own TTS audio instead.
limitations: Read speech by students/academics, not TTS or broadcast; Thai per-language syllable rate not found in the main text.

title: Towards an integrated understanding of speaking rate in conversation
authors: Jiahong Yuan, Mark Liberman, Christopher Cieri
key_findings: Interspeech 2006; large English and Chinese telephone-conversation corpora.
English overall average 196 wpm (conversations range 111-291); net rate excluding silences 236 wpm; turn-wise 164 wpm.
Rate rises sharply for turns of 1-7 words, level for ~8-30 words.
Topic shifts English rate ~152 to ~170 wpm; older speakers slower; males ~2% faster; important/unpredictable parts spoken slower.
practical_applications: Very short lines are spoken faster per word; do not estimate duration of 1-3-word lines from a per-word rate.
limitations: Conversation (dialogue), not narration; English/Chinese only.

title: Universals and cultural variation in turn-taking in conversation
authors: Tanya Stivers et al.
key_findings: All languages avoid overlap and minimise silence between turns; languages differ in mean response gap within about 250 ms of the cross-language mean.
Same factors predict faster/slower responses in every language.
practical_applications: In written dialogue for TTS/animation, replies should follow quickly; long gaps signal hesitation/dispreferred answers (use deliberately).
limitations: Question-answer pairs only; read via abstract.

title: A simplest systematics for the organization of turn-taking for conversation
authors: Harvey Sacks, Emanuel A. Schegloff, Gail Jefferson
key_findings: Turn-taking is locally managed, party-administered, interactionally controlled and recipient-designed; turn-constructional + turn-allocation components minimise gaps and overlaps.
practical_applications: Real dialogue is short turns, built for this listener, with handover cues (questions, tags); scripted dialogue that is paragraph-long speeches sounds written.
limitations: Foundational theory; read via abstract/summary.

title: Using uh and um in spontaneous speaking
authors: Herbert H. Clark, Jean E. Fox Tree
key_findings: Cognition (2002). Fillers-as-words: 'uh' announces a minor delay, 'um' a major delay (London-Lund corpus).
Contested: Language Log notes coder perception vs acoustic measurement differences.
practical_applications: A small, deliberate filler/discourse marker can make dialogue sound spoken and signal thinking; in VO narration fillers usually add length without meaning.
limitations: English; citation volume/pages differ across databases (left blank); read via summaries.

title: Variation across Speech and Writing
authors: Douglas Biber
key_findings: Cambridge University Press. Statistical (multi-feature/multi-dimension) analysis of co-occurring linguistic features distinguishing spoken and written genres.
practical_applications: 'Written style' is a cluster of features (long noun phrases, nominalisations, dense modifiers), not one feature - a checker should combine several signals.
limitations: Book not read; dimension names not confirmed this session.

title: Verbal redundancy in multimedia learning environments: A meta-analysis
authors: Olusola O. Adesope, John C. Nesbit
key_findings: Journal of Educational Psychology 104:250-263.
Spoken+written presentations outperformed spoken-only; did not differ from written-only.
Citing studies report that brief on-screen keywords summarising narration were particularly helpful.
practical_applications: On-screen text = short keywords of the VO, not a full transcript, when visuals also need attention (exception: accessibility captions).
limitations: Learning settings; read via summaries.

title: Reducing verbal redundancy in multimedia learning: An undesired desirable difficulty?
authors: Carole L. Yue, Elizabeth Ligon Bjork, Robert A. Bjork
key_findings: Journal of Educational Psychology (2013). On-screen text identical to narration impaired learning; slightly discrepant (abridged) text produced an advantage (per summary).
practical_applications: Subtitles that are shortened versions of the VO are defensible; word-for-word paragraphs over complex visuals are not.
limitations: Read via search summary; title from PDF filename context.

title: Video Captions Benefit Everyone
authors: Morton Ann Gernsbacher
key_findings: Policy Insights from the Behavioral and Brain Sciences 2(1):195-202.
More than 100 studies: captions improve comprehension, attention and memory; especially helpful in a non-native language.
practical_applications: Burn-in captions on every VO clip (muted feeds, older viewers, accessibility).
limitations: Critics: many studies use foreign-language captions, special populations or self-report; redundancy principle suggests caution (see WatsonLB).

title: 'Video Captions Benefit Everyone': An Investigation
authors: Andrew Watson (Learning and the Brain blog)
key_findings: Argues supporting studies often involve foreign-language captions, at-risk learners, college students or self-report; cognitive load theory suggests caution for typical learners.
practical_applications: Keep captions short and synced; do not add a second competing text layer.
limitations: Blog critique; not peer-reviewed.

title: Federal Plain Language Guidelines (plainlanguage.gov) - 'Write short sentences' and quick-reference tips
authors: Plain Language Action and Information Network (US)
key_findings: Official guidelines for the US Plain Writing Act of 2010.
'Express only one idea in each sentence.'
Archived quick tips: aim for an average of 20 words per sentence, no sentence over 40 words.
practical_applications: Written-copy threshold: avg <=20 words, max 40; for the ear go shorter (see SCRIPT_CHECKER).
limitations: Guideline/consensus, not experimental; English word counts; the 20/40 figure found in archived quick tips, not confirmed in the current page.

title: Content design: Writing for GOV.UK
authors: Government Digital Service (UK)
key_findings: Plain English mandatory; write for a 9-year-old reading age (based on UK average reading age, not a child audience).
Specialist and legal content can and should still be plain; explain needed terms.
practical_applications: Even expert topics (optics, lens tech) get plain wording plus one explained term.
limitations: House style; a '25 words' sentence limit often attributed to GOV.UK was NOT found this session.

title: CDC Clear Communication Index - User Guide and Score Sheet
authors: US Centers for Disease Control and Prevention
key_findings: 20 items scored 0/1, scaled to 100; 90+ passes.
One main message (a topic is not a message), placed at the top; a call to action for the primary audience; main message and CTA in active voice.
Index is a planning aid; does not replace pretesting with the audience.
practical_applications: SCRIPT_CHECKER rules: single main message, early placement, CTA aimed at the viewer, active voice.
limitations: Health print/web materials; research-based index but scoring thresholds are institutional.

title: Using alternative statistical formats for presenting risks and risk reductions
authors: Elie A. Akl et al.
key_findings: Cochrane review, 35 studies / 83 comparisons.
Natural frequencies understood better than probabilities: SMD 0.69 [0.45, 0.93].
Relative risk reduction perceived larger and more persuasive than ARR/NNT, with no better understanding than ARR; authors warn RRR may mislead.
practical_applications: Health scripts: say '1 in 10 people' (natural frequency), give absolute numbers; avoid 'reduces risk by 50%' without the baseline.
limitations: Mostly hypothetical scenarios; read via abstract.

title: Effectiveness and acceptability of interventions to improve readability of patient healthcare materials: A narrative systematic review
authors: J. Dunnett, J. Holkham, A. Trebacz, C. Baldasera, C. Francis, L. Dawson, R. Swiers, F. Christie-De-Jong
key_findings: Public Health; 30 studies (2014-2024), mostly USA.
Simplified language, structured formatting and visuals improved understanding and preference.
Evidence on adherence and health outcomes mixed; study quality generally low.
practical_applications: Plain language is justified for comprehension; do not promise behaviour change from wording alone.
limitations: Narrative (not quantitative) synthesis; read via summary page.

title: Click bait: Forward-reference as lure in online news headlines
authors: Jonas Nygaard Blom, Kenneth Reinecke Hansen
key_findings: Journal of Pragmatics 76:87-100; 100,000 headlines from ten Danish news sites.
Forward-reference (pronouns 'this', adverbs, definite articles, ellipsis, imperatives, questions) used to create anticipation; strongest in commercial/tabloid media without paywalls.
practical_applications: Detect forward-reference hooks ('this one thing...', 'you won't believe') and require the payoff early in the content.
limitations: Describes usage, does not test effectiveness; Danish corpus.

title: The Upworthy Research Archive, a time series of 32,487 experiments in U.S. media
authors: J. Nathan Matias, Kevin Munger, Marianne Aubin Le Quere, Charles Ebersole
key_findings: Scientific Data 8:195. 32,487 headline/image A/B tests (2013-2015), 150,817 arms, ~538 million assignments; clicks and impressions per arm.
Correction: randomisation likely compromised for ~22% of tests (Jun 2013-Jan 2014).
practical_applications: Headline 'rules' should be tested against data like this, not lore; effects are platform- and era-specific.
limitations: Dataset paper - contains no general headline rule; US 2013-2015 clicks only.

title: Aggregation, Clickbait and Their Effect on Perceptions of Journalistic Credibility and Quality
authors: Logan Molyneux, Mark Coddington
key_findings: Journalism Practice 14(4):429-446; two online experiments.
Clickbait headlines lowered perceived credibility and quality, but the effect was small; writing proficiency mattered more.
practical_applications: Over-promising hooks carry a small credibility cost; good writing matters more.
limitations: News context; read via abstract.

title: The (Null) Effects of Clickbait Headlines on Polarization, Trust, and Learning
authors: Kevin Munger, Mario Luca, Jonathan Nagler, Joshua Tucker
key_findings: Public Opinion Quarterly 84(1):49-73; MTurk and Facebook-ad samples.
Older people and non-Democrats showed higher preference for clickbait; reading clickbait vs traditional headlines did not change polarisation, retention or media trust.
practical_applications: Clickbait is neither a proven win nor a proven disaster; judge hooks on honesty and match with content.
limitations: US political news.

title: Effects of age and hearing sensitivity on the comprehension of rapid speech (review and related studies, via secondary summary)
authors: Arthur Wingfield and colleagues; related: Gordon-Salant et al.
key_findings: Older adults are especially sensitive to time-compressed (fast) speech; hearing loss adds a further penalty.
Context and inserted pauses between words/phrases reduce age differences.
Lab time-compressed speech overestimates older adults' handling of naturally fast speech (PMC studies).
practical_applications: For 50+ audiences (presbyopia content) slow the VO and insert pauses at phrase boundaries rather than speeding up to fit time.
limitations: Secondary summary of the review plus several PMC primary studies; exact title/citation not verified.

title: Quick Guide: Writing a radio news script
authors: Media Helping Media
key_findings: Write for the ear (heard once): simple words, short sentences; conversational; lead with the most important point; active voice; round numbers ('nearly two thousand'); title before name; only commas and full stops; read aloud for breath and tongue-twisters; phonetic spellings for hard names.
practical_applications: Directly encoded as VO rules in SCRIPT_CHECKER (numbers, punctuation, read-aloud test).
limitations: Practitioner guidance, English broadcast.

title: Dialogue: The Art of Verbal Action for Page, Stage, and Screen
authors: Robert McKee
key_findings: Twelve/Hachette, July 2016. Treats dialogue as action (characters do things to each other with words) across screen, stage, page.
practical_applications: Craft frame for subtext rule: each line should do something (persuade, hide, attack), not report information.
limitations: Book not read (bibliographic); one review says it gives hard rules rather than adaptable advice.

title: Message Design Choices Don't Make Much Difference to Persuasiveness and Can't Be Counted On - Not Even When Moderating Conditions Are Specified
authors: Daniel J. O'Keefe, Hans Hoeken
key_findings: 1,149 studies of 30 message-design variations; median main-effect r = .10; prediction intervals frequently include negative effects even under moderators.
Narrative vs non-narrative r = .067, k = 34.
practical_applications: No copy formula (hook type, CTA wording) is guaranteed; the checker flags risks, it does not predict performance.
limitations: First ~100k characters read.

title: Impact of narratives on persuasion in health communication: A meta-analysis
authors: Fuyuan Shen, Vivian C. Sheer, Ruobing Li
key_findings: 25 studies, N = 9,330; r = .063; audio/video narratives significant, print not; detection/prevention yes, cessation no.
practical_applications: Medical-communication scripts: narrative works better for 'go get checked' than 'stop doing X'.
limitations: Read via summaries; substantial heterogeneity (O'Keefe & Hoeken).

title: Similar information rates across languages, despite divergent speech rates (press release)
authors: CNRS / Université Lumière Lyon 2
key_findings: Lay summary of Coupé et al. 2019: ~39 bits/s across languages; 5-8 bits per syllable; faster languages are less dense.
Gives no Thai-specific figure.
practical_applications: Do not transfer an English or Spanish syllable rate to Thai.
limitations: Press release.

title: You won't believe what's in this paper! Clickbait, relevance, and the curiosity gap
authors: Kate Scott
key_findings: Relevance-theoretic account of clickbait and the curiosity gap; discusses Blom & Hansen's forward-reference categories (per search summary).
practical_applications: A hook creates an expectation of relevance; if the content does not pay it off, the viewer's effort is wasted - the mechanism behind 'hook must match content'.
limitations: Only the listing/search summary seen; journal and year not verified.
